title: Invisible in the data: how London universities are failing disabled students through ambition without accountability

The post Invisible in the data: how London universities are failing disabled students through ambition without accountability  appeared first on HEPI.
full_text:
This blog was kindly authored by Ella Malik, Research Assistant, and Dr Helen Coulshed, Associate Vice Dean (Assessment and Quality Assurance) in the Faculty of Natural, Mathematical and Engineering Sciences and Senior Lecturer in Chemistry Education, both at King’s College London.

In 2025, the National Students Survey (NSS) recorded lower positivity scores amongst disabled students across every domain. That same year, an Office for Students (OfS) workshop found that only 15.2% of providers systematically evaluate the effectiveness of reasonable adjustments, while 60% rely on informal or ad hoc processes. Without systematic evaluation, institutions cannot determine whether their support is effective, and outcome gaps are likely to persist undetected.

To understand how universities are responding, we audited Access and Participation Plans (APPs) from 16 London-based higher education institutions, spanning pre-92 and post-92 providers, specialist institutions, and research-intensive universities.

Why Disabled Students Are Hard to See in the Data

In 2023, the OfS reformed the APP framework around a risk-based model. Under this model, institutions are required to identify specific outcome gaps, provide evidence of their causes and set proportionate targets in response – replacing broad aspirational commitments with measurable ones. For disabled students, however, this model has structural limitations.

Unlike other underrepresented groups, disabled students often require a diagnosis to be recognised in institutional data and access support. Diagnosis rates vary significantly by gender, income, and ethnicity, and students who are awaiting assessment or face financial or cultural barriers to obtaining one may not appear in the figures that drive institution planning.

Aggregated reporting compounds this. When all disability types are grouped into a single category, differences between subgroups, such as between students on the autism spectrum and students with ADHD, can be obscured. An institution may show no measurable gap at the aggregate level while significant disparities exist within it. In this way, the absence of a recorded gap does not confirm the absence of disadvantage.

Patterns Across the Sample

Most institutions in our sample acknowledge disability as a concern: 13 of 16 identified it as a risk factor, and 15 of 16 included at least one linked intervention strategy. Two institutions did not designate disability as a prioritised risk, but both maintained disability-linked provision. This is consistent with the OfS whole-provider approach, which recognises that small cohort sizes can make disadvantage statistically invisible and encourages institutions to embed inclusive provision into standard practice without requiring a formal risk designation at every lifecycle stage.

However, this acknowledgement did not consistently translate into commitment. Only 8 of 16 institutions set numerical targets for their disability related intervention strategies. The remaining eight classified disability as an ‘area for monitoring’ or set no targets. Five institutions had already disaggregated disability types, identified a specific condition with a significant gap at a lifecycle stage, and still set no target to reduce it.

To analyse variation across the sample, we developed a Granularity Index with three tiers. Tier 1 institutions set intersectional targets combining disability type with other characteristics such as age or ethnicity, Tier 2 institutions set targets for a single specific condition, and Tier 3 institutions used aggregated disability data. Tier 1 and 2 institutions linked their disaggregated data to condition-specific support. One Tier 1 institution, for example, set intersectional targets for minoritised ethnic students with mental health conditions, and developed specific interventions including a psychoeducation programme and anti-stigma workshop aimed at increasing help-seeking behaviour. Tier 3 institutions focus instead on systemic change through broad, aggregate targets.

The differences between Tier 1 and 2 universities and Tier 3 institutions reflect a strategic choice between condition-specific support and systemic inclusive-by-design frameworks. But this raises a practical question: inclusive-by-design approaches benefit students without a formal diagnosis who would otherwise be invisible in the data, but applying them without disaggregation can mask the very disparities they are meant to address. How can institutions reconcile these two facts?

What Effective Practice Looks Like

The variation across the sample points to two recurring limitations: students without a formal diagnosis are often excluded from support and absent from outcome data, and aggregated disability reporting conceals differences between subgroups. The strongest APPs addressed both directly.

One institution removed the requirement for medical or diagnostic evidence to register for bespoke disability support, reducing the barrier for students awaiting assessment or unable to obtain a diagnosis. Critically, this did not come at the cost of analytical precision: UAL continues to collect condition-specific outcome data, meaning broader access to support does not prevent the institution from identifying where targeted intervention is still needed.

Disaggregation by disability type alone, however, does not account for disadvantage that compounds across multiple characteristics. Another institution addressed this by applying logistic regression at each lifecycle stage to identify characteristics independently associated with risk and isolating the specific combinations that predict disadvantage. Mandating this kind of intersectional analysis as a standard component of APP development would shift the burden of proof: rather than waiting for compounded disadvantage to appear in headline figures, institutions would be required to actively test for it.

Together, these examples illustrate that improving outcomes for disabled students is not solely a question of what support is offered, but of how precisely institutions can identify who needs it and why. That precision depends on the quality of the analytical commitments institutions make, and this is where the current framework has a measurable gap.

Classifying disability as an ‘area for monitoring’ is not inherently problematic, but it requires specification. Institutions should be able to state what data is being collected, what threshold would trigger a target commitment, and what evidence would indicate that no further action is required. Without this, monitoring records awareness of a potential problem rather than a structured plan to address it. For students whose disadvantage is already difficult to see in the data, the difference between monitoring and acting is not an administrative one.

title: Academy trust pays out after Prevent threat over children’s Palestine badges
summary:
Lion Academy Trust apologises after threatening four pupils in east London with referral to counter-extremism scheme

full_text:
An academy trust will pay out tens of thousands in compensation to four children who were told they could be referred to Prevent for wearing Palestine flag badges to school.

The school, part of Lion Academy Trust, has issued a formal apology after it sent letters to the children’s parents saying they might be referred to the counter-extremism programme or to local hate crime teams.

The issue dates back to November 2023 when the children’s school, Barclay primary school in Leyton, east London, held a non-uniform fundraising day for Children in Need.

The four children, all British Muslims aged between six and 10 at the time, attended wearing items displaying Palestinian colours or the Palestinian flag, in memory of children who had been killed in Gaza and those who continued to suffer during the conflict, which was ongoing at the time.

One child wore a Children in Need Pudsey sticker featuring a bow tie in Palestinian colours. Another wore a homemade badge bearing the Palestinian flag and colours.

Parents of the four children said they had repeatedly asked the school to apologise for their treatment of the children and had launched a legal challenge when none was forthcoming.

At a hearing at Central London county court on Thursday, the court heard that the academy trust had now made a formal apology to the children and their families and would pay them substantial compensation.

Lawyers for the children alleged direct discrimination, indirect discrimination and harassment on grounds including race, ethnicity, religion and belief, together with breaches of their rights to freedom of expression and freedom of thought, conscience and belief.

Shahid Achhala, the father of one of the children, said: “What happened to our son was deeply disturbing and should never have happened to any child. He was just eight years old, expressing compassion and solidarity with children suffering in Gaza, including members of his own extended family. Instead of being supported and protected by the school entrusted with his care, he was deliberately subjected to mistreatment that caused him considerable emotional distress.

“For almost three years, we have had to fight legally for accountability and an acknowledgment of the wrongs we believe were committed. While we welcome Lion Academy Trust’s apology, we cannot overlook the distress caused to our son and our family, or the fact that this matter could have been resolved long time ago.”

The families were represented by law firm Leigh Day and supported in their legal claim by Prevent Watch, which provides casework support to individuals and families affected by the Prevent duty.

Layla Aitlhadj, a director at Prevent Watch, said: “In this case, parents who were protecting their children’s rights were told that their concerns were ‘false and malicious’. They held firm through three years of pressure. Today the families, and the wider community who stood with them, have been vindicated.”

The academy trust has been approached for comment.

full_text:
For Maria, the hardest part of having a child with complex needs has been the grief: mourning the life she had imagined for her son, for her family – and coming to terms with how lonely the reality of parenting him can be.

“There are wonderful days but there are very hard ones too,” she added, tears coursing down her face.

Thanks to a school dedicated to children and young people with multiple, severe and complex special needs, however, Maria is not alone any more.

Already the recipient of seven consecutive “outstanding” Ofsted ratings, the Swiss Cottage School, Development and Research Centre, operated by the local authority in Camden, has now received worldwide recognition as winner of the World’s Best School prize for community collaboration. It is the first time a school in England has won the prize.

The school has attracted the attention of those in government: the education secretary, Lucy Powell, said it was “a case in point of what we want to replicate through our Send reforms: a system where every child feels they belong and can access the support they need, close to home, without a fight”.

On paper, the Swiss Cottage school is just one of more than 1,000 state-funded special schools in England, catering for the country’s 10,000-plus children with profound developmental and learning difficulties.

But in reality, “Swiss”, as its families fondly call it, is run very differently. “Swiss has become our second family,” said Maria. “Support for children with complex needs is split across education, healthcare and social services. But Swiss does it all for us.”

“You have no idea,” she added, breathing out a great sigh of relief, “how much stress and weight that removes from parents’ shoulders.”

Instead of focusing solely on teaching their own pupils, Swiss is also different in that it operates an integrated research and training hub, leads teacher training programmes and conducts educational research.

It shares its best practices with hundreds of mainstream and special schools across the UK and internationally: over the last year alone, it has had delegations from South America, Uzbekistan, Saudi Arabia and Sweden.

Syra Sowe, head of the school, is reluctant to name names, but several UK schools have changed their teacher training, curriculums and planning, she said, after Swiss’s input. “Just to be clear, we don’t just use these partnerships to disseminate best practice,” she added. “We also learn from others.”

Until Maria found Swiss, her family were stuck in a nightmare. Her 18-year-old son, Alex, has Sotos syndrome, a rare genetic condition that has left him struggling with epilepsy, scoliosis, autism and severe developmental delays.

“Before Alex came here, no one understood him and he was raging. He hit, kicked and bit everyone; he was beyond therapy,” she said.

No nursery would keep Alex for more than an hour before calling his mother to collect him. By contrast, he has never had to leave Swiss early.

“This school has given him back his childhood. They immediately saw behind his disabilities to a child who needed an education – and had the right to an education,” Maria said. “He’s now a sociable young man who’s curious about everything, and who loves learning.”

Alex will leave Swiss this September and Maria is determined that his education will continue. Her son, she is resolved, will not become one of the approximately 38% of Neets (not in education, employment or training) who have multiple or complex needs – roughly translating to about 380,000 young people.

With the help of Swiss, Maria is confident this will not happen to Alex. It is a matter of intense pride to Sowe that her students all, without exception, go on to further education, training or specialist support. “We don’t produce Neets,” she said. “Any limits we think these children have are actually limits on our own imaginations and ambitions for them.”

The potential can be unclear to the untrained eye but teachers at the school see it clearly. On a tour of the school, one pupil grabbed the camera of the Guardian photographer and smelled it. Then he took Sowe’s lanyard and sniffed it too.

Grinning, he leapt back to the plateglass window of the school’s roof garden, happily slapping it, rocking and making a series of vocalisations.

Sowe’s reaction was one of pride. “That child has the most incredible olfactory sensitivity and olfactory memory,” she said. “He virtually navigates the world through smell; he’s amazing.”

Key to drawing out each child’s individual potential is the bespoke curriculum the school provides for each child, adjusted every week around the child’s evolving individual communication, cognitive and physical needs, at meetings between teaching staff, therapists, specialists, nurses, physiotherapists and the NHS Camhs professionals embedded in the school.

The school pushes the conventional boundaries of a special school in other interesting ways: rather than preparing pupils for a world they may struggle to access, its Employ ME programme not only gives its young people experience of working in the outside world – but aims to give the outside world experience of their unique skills and strengths.

“A key part of what we do is teach the universe how incredible our young people are,” said Sowe. “And what they have to offer, so the universe has more to offer to them when they leave us.”

title: Will More International Students Enroll Next Year?
summary:
Will More International Students Enroll Next Year?
kathryn.palmer… Thu, 11/19/2026 - 03:00 AM

Although international enrollment is down this fall, preliminary data from Common App shows a 9 percent uptick in the number of international applicants for the 2026–27 academic year.

Byline(s)
Kathryn Palmer
full_text:
The share of international students applying to colleges in the United States is on the rebound so far this year, according to new data that Common App released this week.

Compared to the same point in the application cycle last year, the number of international students applying to college through the Common App is up 9 percent this year—after decreasing by the same proportion between the 2024–25 and 2025–26 academic years. And that puts international student applicants back on their post-pandemic upward trajectory.

Between the 2022–23 academic year and the current one, the number of international student applicants who used Common App climbed from 65,645 to 78,986, peaking at 80,095 in 2024. According to the report, students from Europe are leading that growth, with a 15 percent increase in applications since the 2022–23 academic year. In that same period, applications from Oceania grew 11 percent, Asia 9 percent, the Americas 8 percent and Africa 6 percent.

The application rebound isn’t the only sign that international students may be warming back up to the prospect of studying in the United States in the wake of the Trump administration’s crackdown on student visas. In the week after Democrats won control of Congress earlier this month, Studyportals, an online platform that helps international students search and compare programs, reported a 40 percent increase in the number of web-page views for on-campus programs based at a college or university in the United States.

While that may sound hopeful to colleges reliant on international enrollment revenues to balance their budgets, those indicators haven’t yet translated into enrollment increases. According to preliminary data that the Institute of International Education published Monday, overall international enrollment declined 9 percent between fall 2025 and fall 2026, a significantly steeper drop than the 3 percent decrease from fall 2024 to fall 2025.

And the new report from Common App is just a narrow glimpse of what international student enrollment could look like come next year. For one thing, the college application portal’s members include fewer than half of all four-year institutions. In addition, the report released this week captures one moment in time: It compares data from the 2026–27 application cycle through Nov. 1, the first major deadline, to the data from the same point in time last year. Common App will release monthly updates through March, the last major deadline of the college application cycle.

In addition to looking at international students, the report identified some of the following application-related trends between Nov. 1, 2025, and Nov. 1, 2026.

The number of first-year domestic applicants remained relatively flat, increasing from 908,867 to 913,107—less than 1 percent.

The volume of applications is up over all, with 63 percent of colleges that use Common App reporting an increase or stable application volume compared to 37 percent that saw a decrease. Most of the increase was driven by a 14 percent growth in applications to the most selective institutions and the same level of growth in applications to private institutions. Applications to public institutions increased by 3 percent year over year.

title: Could a New HBCU Campus Open in California?
summary:
Could a New HBCU Campus Open in California?
Olivia.sanchez Thu, 11/19/2026 - 03:00 AM
Byline(s)
Olivia Sanchez
full_text:
California has the fifth-largest Black population in the nation, but no historically Black college or university of its own. To attend an HBCU, California students would have to move halfway across the country—the westernmost HBCU is in San Antonio—and pay out-of-state tuition rates.

Now the Oakland HBCU Task Force, a coalition of education and business leaders and public officials, is trying to serve Black students from the Bay Area by establishing a West Coast satellite campus of an existing HBCU.

They believe their city, where nearly one in five residents are Black, is the right place to establish such a campus. Morris Brown and Paul Quinn Colleges have expressed interest in opening a California satellite in the past, but currently it remains unclear which HBCU would be involved.

In a feasibility study published Wednesday, the HR&A Advisors, a national advisory firm, said Oakland was well suited for an HBCU because of the varied professional industries in the region and evolving workforce demand, opportunities to partner with Peralta Community College District, and the city’s cultural history. Introducing an HBCU satellite campus there would boost bachelor’s degree attainment among Oaklanders, draw new residents, create jobs and benefit the city’s economy, according to the report.

Derek Fleming, a co-author of the feasibility study and senior adviser at HR&A Advisors, said in a statement that bringing an HBCU campus to Oakland could also offer a new opportunity for other HBCUs to expand.

“By connecting Oakland’s educational institutions, industry employers, cultural assets, and underutilized real estate, this initiative can expand access to higher education, create pathways to quality careers, and catalyze new economic activity and investment in Oakland,” Fleming said. “The path forward begins by building partnerships before buildings, allowing institutions to demonstrate success and grow sustainably.”

In recent years, Vanderbilt University and Carnegie Mellon University have established satellite operations in the Bay Area with a focus on work-based learning. The advisers outlined plans for a similar approach, at least initially, with the hopes of launching a pilot program by 2028 and establishing a permanent campus by 2030.

As part of the feasibility study, the task force met with local high schoolers and leaders, many of whom expressed support, according to the report.

Oakland Mayor Barbara Lee said in a statement that an HBCU in the city would keep students close, help the economy and “extend Oakland’s legacy as a center of Black culture and power.”

“Oakland’s young Black students deserve the best, and HBCUs are the best,” Lee said.

title: Why Scheduling Is Essential for Transfer Student Success
summary:
Why Scheduling Is Essential for Transfer Student Success
quintina.barne… Thu, 11/19/2026 - 03:00 AM

Students won’t stick around for long if they can’t get the classes they need.

Byline(s)
Paul Dosal
full_text:
If you ask 100 community college students about their plans for the future, 80 of them will say they’re planning to transfer to a four-year institution. The number who actually do? National data suggests that it’s only 32. Of those, just 15—fewer than half of those who make the jump to a four-year institution—will go on to earn a bachelor’s degree.

Transfer students are hopeful, resilient and fully capable of planning their educational journeys. Many start at a community college for sound strategic reasons, such as cost or location. The issue isn’t a lack of ambition or planning. It’s that institutions, often without realizing it, have put obstacles in the transfer pipeline. They haven’t consistently created clearly defined transfer pathways or provided the advising students need along the way.

For far too long, colleges and universities have seen transfer students as a convenient way to fill seats and meet enrollment goals. Yet transfer students are a sizable student population with their own unique challenges. It’s estimated that roughly 40 percent of all undergraduate students transfer at least once during their academic careers. In fall 2024, 13 percent of all continuing and returning undergraduates were transfer students—a number that grew by 4.4 percent in one year. At some institutions, transfer students make up as much as a quarter of undergraduate enrollment.

Students transfer to other institutions for a wide variety of reasons. They want to leave community college for a four-year institution. They have changed their minds about their majors, programs or careers. They need to save money. Or they’re seeking more convenience and flexibility to complete college on their own timeline. A growing number of transfer students are not switching institutions immediately but rather re-entering college after a break of several years, with a majority opting to enroll someplace other than where they started.

Jobs, finances and family responsibilities can increase the difficulty of successfully transferring and completing college. But despite arranging articulation agreements, building completion pathways and improving advising and other student supports, institutions can be their own worst enemies when it comes to transfer students. On average, community college students lose 20 percent of their credits when they transfer to a public four-year institution. Having to repeat classes causes them to spend more time and money to complete their degree. These delays are compounded because colleges are able to provide required courses when students need them only about 15 percent of the time.

This isn’t a student problem. It’s an institutional crisis that drives down student enrollment, retention and graduation.

In a state like Florida, where recurring funding is based in part on improving performance on key metrics—including a three-year transfer student graduation rate—institutions cannot afford to ignore the transfer-student pipeline.

A new playbook offers a way forward for institutions seeking to unlock success for their transfer students through better scheduling that ensures courses are available when students need them and are aligned with program pathways.

This process begins with institutions understanding their transfer students by learning more about their backgrounds and goals and determining how they experience the academic schedule. At the same time, institutions should define effective scheduling for transfer students and set specific, measurable and intentional goals for improving transfer outcomes.

To build effective schedules, institutions should closely examine program-level data to see where transfer students are enrolling and where they’re having success. These metrics can help align instructional and faculty capacity to student demand.

Institutions should identify transfer-critical courses that are required to complete majors or serve as prerequisites for upper-level work. Because these gateway courses are potential bottlenecks, institutions should ensure that they are taught by multiple instructors and offered in several different modalities at different times of the day and on different days of the week. Building annual course schedules instead of taking the traditional semester-by-semester approach can help institutions determine when they should offer courses and in which modalities.

After schedules are published and students register for classes, institutions should continue to monitor multiple metrics and create feedback loops that can improve scheduling efforts and stabilize academic pathways.

Florida Gulf Coast University built its student success movement on strategic enrollment planning and management, including more clearly defined curriculum pathways for transfer students. A new team, part of a universitywide initiative to improve institutional performance, will focus on transfer student success by working with FGCU faculty and their counterparts in the Florida College System to streamline transfer pathways and ensure more community college students are fully prepared to succeed at a comprehensive regional public university.

Strategic course scheduling requires more than just allocating faculty and financial resources and classroom space. It’s about creating an institutional culture that values success for all learners, including transfer students, to make sure that students can get the courses they need when they need them so they can jump successfully to a new institution, make timely progress toward their degrees and graduate on their schedules.

title: Rethinking the Student Success Playbook
summary:
Rethinking the Student Success Playbook
Joshua.Bay Thu, 11/19/2026 - 03:00 AM

At Student Success US, campus leaders explored what it takes to turn student-centered ideas into meaningful institutional change.

Byline(s)
Joshua Bay
full_text:
SALT LAKE CITY—Student success has become an increasingly central priority for colleges and universities as conversations shift beyond growing enrollment to ensuring students have the support they need to complete their degrees and thrive beyond higher education. Behind those efforts, however, stand faculty, staff and administrators whose demanding and often overlooked work is essential to helping students reach their goals.

Hundreds of student success leaders from institutions across the nation gathered this week for the annual Student Success US conference, a collaboration between Inside Higher Ed and our parent company, Times Higher Education, in partnership with the University of Utah. Speakers shared insights into the challenges students face both in and outside the classroom, highlighting opportunities for colleges and universities to rethink how they support students throughout their academic journeys and prepare them for life after graduation.

In his opening remarks, Geoffrey Landward, commissioner of higher education for the Utah System of Higher Education, argued that the value of higher education lies not only in the credentials students earn but also in the skills and opportunities they gain to build better lives and contribute to their communities.

“Trust is not built through enrolling students,” Landward said. “Trust is built by ensuring that they understand that there is going to be a return on the investment that they’re making and that you care about that return. You care about ensuring that they have the kind of experience that allows them to tell their friends, their family and their children that college is worth it.”

Throughout the conference, speakers explored how institutions can gain and maintain that trust, sharing strategies for addressing students’ evolving needs and strengthening the support systems that help them succeed. Discussions covered everything from putting student-centered design into practice and approaching student well-being more holistically to overcoming institutional barriers to innovation.

Turn feedback into action: In a panel moderated by Inside Higher Ed Editor in Chief Sara Custer, speakers discussed what student-centered design looks like in practice.

Jillian Kinzie, associate director of the National Survey of Student Engagement at Indiana University Bloomington, emphasized that evidence gathered directly from students should inform institutions’ approaches to student success. She also highlighted the value of involving students in interpreting findings, allowing them to provide context, challenge assumptions and offer perspectives grounded in their own experiences.

“To me, when evidence is only held by a small cadre of individuals on campus, it tends to be siloed and inaccessible,” Kinzie said. “When we share and actually sit down with others and make sense of the data, that’s when it really latches on.”

Mitzi Montoya, provost and executive vice president at the University of Utah, offered an example from her institution, where administrators discovered that 15 student surveys were being conducted simultaneously. Although each survey served an important purpose, she noted the sheer volume risked overwhelming students and contributing to “survey fatigue.”

“We collect a lot of data—we all collect a lot of data—but are we using it? And how do we turn it into something actionable?” Montoya said.

Share what works: In another panel, Bridget Burns, founding chief executive officer of the University Innovation Alliance, and Nancy Zimpher, president of the National Association of Higher Education Systems, examined how institutional structures and long-standing practices can hinder efforts to improve student outcomes, particularly with regard to fostering innovation and collaboration across campuses.

Zimpher highlighted the challenges facing higher education systems and organizations seeking to drive institutional change, pointing to perceptions of bureaucracy and the limitations of funding models that rely heavily on grants and contracts.

“The problem with that model is that people don’t like us, and they think of us as bureaucratic and top-down,” Zimpher said. “We live almost unfortunately on grants and contracts, which means it’s hard to build the strength of the organization … because all that money goes out the door to help you do your work and nothing stays behind to run the backbone.”

Burns emphasized that meaningful innovation requires institutions to move beyond campus-level competition and create environments where they can openly share challenges, failures and effective practices.

“When I’m talking about system change, I’m thinking about how every institution is set up to be obsessed with the boundaries of their own campus [and] to believe that what you’re doing is the greatest,” Burns said.

“The design of American higher education is set up for you to treat good ideas as a trade secret,” she said. “That is the kind of system change we want to change—what is incentivized, what [do] you talk about and how do you actually know what the right stuff is to do?”

Rethink student wellness: In breakout sessions, conversations explored how institutions can take a more holistic approach to student well-being, from reimagining campus housing as a wellness ecosystem to developing shared competencies for financial fluency.

Rebecca Caldwell, director of residential well-being at Virginia Tech, emphasized that campus housing should be viewed as a foundation of student wellness rather than a separate component of the college experience, particularly as institutions face growing demands to address students’ mental health needs with limited resources. At Virginia Tech, that means refocusing residential well-being efforts around three core goals: strengthening students’ sense of belonging, reducing loneliness and fostering flourishing.

“University belonging and social connection are very positively correlated with students’ mental health,” Caldwell said. “We want to promote positive and healthy behaviors because promoting that sense of belonging … is going to change your residential environment.”

In a separate session, Phil Schuman, president of the Higher Education Financial Wellness Alliance, and Julie Payne-Kirchmeier, president and chief executive officer of Edgefield Group LLC, introduced the alliance’s emerging national competency framework, aimed at establishing a shared understanding of what students should know and be able to do to achieve financial competency.

Schuman outlined four core domains of the framework: financial influences and decision-making, financial management and stability, financial planning and future readiness, and informed financial consumer and systems navigation.

“When we look at this framework, we’re not saying that a financial wellness office needs to be responsible for all of these things. In fact, a lot of institutions are probably doing a lot of these things already,” Schuman said. “We want universities to start using this framework to help map against it, and see what they are providing, where the gaps are and how they can figure out how to address those gaps for their students.”

Payne-Kirchmeier emphasized that financial wellness encompasses more than financial knowledge alone, noting that the alliance recently opened applications for a cohort of 12 institutions to explore how the financial competencies can strengthen student learning, financial decision-making and well-being across different higher education settings.

“This is a comprehensive issue that has emotion, culture, history, skill, knowledge and changing policy around it,” Payne-Kirchmeier said. “We knew we needed to make sure, much like pilots are, that our students are competent in multiple dimensions.”

title: Senate appropriations committee proposes $15B in additional Pell Grant funding
summary: The Republican-led bill for fiscal 2027 would also keep funding flat for the U.S. Department of Education’s Office for Civil Rights.
full_text:
This audio is auto-generated. Please let us know if you have feedback.

Dive Brief:

The Pell Grant program would receive $15 billion of additional funding in fiscal 2027 under a bill put forward by the Senate’s appropriations committee this week.

The money is intended to address a shortfall projected to reach $16.9 billion by the end of fiscal 2027. The proposal would keep the maximum grant at$7,395 in the 2027-28 academic year.

The Republican-led committee’s billalso rebukes many of the cuts to the U.S. Department of Education sought by the Trump administration and the House. The proposal would keep funding flat for two key higher education programs — Federal Work-Study at $1.2 billionand Federal Supplemental Educational Opportunity Grants at $910 million.

Dive Insight:

Congress has until Dec. 11 to either pass a budget or another stopgap funding measure to avoid a government shutdown.

But the midterm election results have increased the pressure on Republicans, who currently control both chambers of Congress. If lawmakers pass another continuing resolution that extends into the new year or if the government shuts down until January, power over the budget will be handed to Democrats.

Against that backdrop, West Virginia Sen. Shelley Moore Capito, chair of the appropriations subcommittee overseeing Education Department funding,said Monday that the bill reflects “priorities that have long enjoyed bipartisan support.”

The Education Department would receive $93.9 billion in discretionary funding in fiscal 2027 under the proposal, a major boost from the $78.8 billion appropriated to the agency in the prior year.

The bill would keep funding for the department’s Office for Civil Rights at $140 million, while Trump’s fiscal 2027 proposal sought to cut OCR’s funding to $91 million.Similarly, the Institute of Education Sciences,the department’s office that collects and analyzes data from colleges and K-12 schools, would get $789.6 million, the same as it did in fiscal 2026. The White House proposed just $261.3 million.

But the education funding bill — released alongside budget proposals for several other federal agencies — left the committee’s Democratic leadership dissatisfied. In a Monday statement, Washington Sen. Patty Murray, vice chair of the appropriations committee, heavily criticized the overall budget bill as being full of “backward funding priorities,” citing the significant increases in defense spending.

She also argued the proposal “fails to rein in this administration” and prevent Trump from politicizing federal grants and moving to dismantle the Education Department.

Murray urged her party members to join her in negotiating with Republicans.

“Democrats cannot accept a topline agreement that delivers a windfall for defense contractors and crumbs for everyone else,” she said.

At least one higher ed group has also urged lawmakers to go further.

Nalia Medina, assistant director of government relations at the National Association of Student Financial Aid Administrators, said Wednesday that it was encouraging to see a proposal to address the Pell Grant program’s shortfall.But she also called for an increase to the maximum Pell Grant, citing its decreased spending power.

title: Meta rethinks 2030 climate goals as AI data centres drive emissions up
summary: Rising data centre energy needs force Meta to review sustainability targets amid growing corporate climate retreat.
full_text:
Meta, the owner of Facebook and Instagram, has said it is reconsidering its 2030 deadline for reaching net-zero emissions because of the artificial intelligence (AI) boom, in the latest sign of a broad corporate retreat from climate pledges.

The company is “re-evaluating our timelines, sequencing and interim milestones, including the 2030 timeframe for our net zero emissions goal”, Rachel Peterson, Meta’s vice president of data centres, and Blair Swedeen, its global head of net zero and sustainability, said in the company’s annual sustainability report on Thursday.

Recommended Stories

list of 3 items

list 1 of 3‘Climate crisis is outrunning us,’ UN chief Guterres says at COP31

list 2 of 3Tensions rise over draft climate deal at COP31

list 3 of 3What’s in the air you breathe? How to stay safe during smog season

end of list

Meta reported that its net carbon-equivalent emissions rose 45 percent in 2025 to 11.8 million tonnes, a figure that is itself based on accounting methods that climate advocates view with scepticism.

“When we set our net zero emissions goal, we anticipated steady growth, falling clean energy costs, and changes in the broader system that would enable progress at the pace we envisioned. The reality has been far more complex,” the executives wrote in the report. They said delivering on Meta’s vision “requires building the infrastructure that powers AI”.

What was the pledge?

In 2020, Meta set a goal of net-zero emissions across its entire value chain by 2030, in line with the Paris Agreement, which aims to hold long-term warming to 1.5C (2.7F) above pre-industrial levels.

Net zero means eliminating emissions as far as possible and buying credits from carbon removal projects to offset those that cannot be eliminated. The value chain covers emissions from sources such as purchased goods and services, as well as capital goods such as equipment, buildings and vehicles.

A study published this week in the journal Nature Sustainability found that 403 of the most powerful data centres in the United States accounted for about 2 percent of the country’s electricity use and a carbon footprint comparable to Denmark’s, the AFP news agency reported.

About 1,200 such “hyperscale” data centres are online, and hundreds more are planned. Globally, data centres used about 415 terawatt hours of electricity in 2024, about 1.5 percent of supply, and that could nearly double by 2030, according to the International Energy Agency.

A wider retreat

During US President Donald Trump’s second term, major American businesses have stepped back from environmental commitments.

The trend is not confined to Big Tech. General Motors, which set a goal of selling only zero-emission vehicles by 2035, backed the Trump administration’s weakening of a fuel economy rule this year.

Walmart acknowledged in 2024 that it would miss its first emissions target. Google, which pledged in 2020 to run on carbon-free energy by 2030, said this year that its emissions were still rising.

Coca-Cola and Pepsi have changed the baseline years for their emissions targets and weakened their ambitions.

title: Former BMI founders launch new international education events company
summary:
Former BMI founders Samir Zaveri and Rupert Merrick have launched a new international education events company, Campus Global, following the closure of BMI earlier this year.

The post Former BMI founders launch new international education events company appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
The UK-based company has announced a program of international student fairs, school visits, counsellor workshops and a scholarship forum for 2027, spanning markets in the Middle East, Latin America, Southeast Asia and Europe.

Zaveri founded BMI in 1987 and worked alongside Merrick for more than 25 years. The pair have taken on the roles of co-founder and president, and co-founder and managing director, respectively.

Zaveri said encouragement from universities, school counsellors and partners following the announcement of BMI’s closure had helped prompt the launch.

“Their encouragement helped give us the confidence to start Campus Global,” he said.

“We bring decades of experience and local knowledge to the new company, and we have the freedom to put fresh ideas into practice.”

We bring decades of experience and local knowledge to the new company, and we have the freedom to put fresh ideas into practice

Samir Zaveri, Campus Global

Merrick said the company was launching at a time of changing student recruitment strategies, with artificial intelligence reshaping how students research study options, visa policies shifting and new destinations emerging.

While digital recruitment strategies and agent relationships remained central to international student recruitment, he said universities were renewing their investment in face-to-face engagement.

“Being there in person lets universities build relationships, answer families’ questions and hear directly what matters to students in that market,” he said.

Campus Global’s program is designed to combine several recruitment activities within individual market visits, allowing university representatives to meet prospective students, school counsellors and scholarship organisations.

The company’s 2027 schedule includes education fairs in Dubai and Abu Dhabi in April and October, alongside a Gulf and Central Asia Counsellor Workshop in Abu Dhabi in April.

In Latin America, six student fairs will take place across Brazil in April, followed by events in Mexico, Colombia, Peru and Brazil in October. International student fairs are also planned for Jakarta and Surabaya in Indonesia in October.

The company will hold a counsellor workshop in Sesimbra, near Lisbon in May, with a further workshop in Dubai in October. A scholarship forum will also take place in Dubai that month.

Campus Global said its counsellor workshops and scholarship forum would include pre-scheduled one-to-one meetings between universities and participants.

The company has also established a counsellor advisory board, chaired by Andy Coxall of EvolveCareers, to give school counsellors a role in shaping its events and discussing issues facing the international counselling community.

title: What the CPT dispute reveals about the promise of a US education
summary:
Changes to US rules governing Curricular Practical Training (CPT) risk limiting international students’ access to work-based learning, while creating uncertainty for universities, argues Shaun Carver.

The post What the CPT dispute reveals about the promise of a US education appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
In 2024, more than 130,000 international students on F-1 visas were authorised to take part in Curricular Practical Training (CPT), the US program that allows them to undertake internships and other work-based learning during their studies. These placements let students apply classroom learning in professional settings while contributing their skills to US organisations.

For many, that opportunity is part of what makes an American education worth the investment.

Then, in August 2026, two Student and Exchange Visitor Program messages narrowed when CPT could be authorised. Under the previous interpretation, an international student could use CPT for an internship that counted toward their degree even when the placement was optional.

The new interpretation says CPT is available only when every student on the same degree must complete practical training to graduate. If students can choose between an internship and a classroom-based alternative, an international student may no longer use CPT for the internship.

Four higher education associations have since filed suit challenging the change, arguing that a long-standing policy was altered without formal rulemaking or time for universities and students to adjust.

Whatever the courts decide, the dispute exposes a wider problem for international education. Students make decisions about where to study and how to finance a degree based partly on the experience they expect to receive. Universities cannot plan responsibly when rules central to that experience change after those commitments have been made.

Practical learning is part of the education

An internship is more than a line on a résumé. When it is designed well, it is a structured part of learning. A student works under supervision, connects the placement to their field and returns to the classroom with a sharper understanding of how ideas operate in practice.

Degree programs preserve choice for good reasons. Two students in the same program may be preparing for different professions, so the most valuable placement for one may not suit the other. Making practical training elective can be a sign of thoughtful curriculum design and does not place it outside the education. The decision to offer an internship alongside a classroom-based option allows universities to respond to different academic goals while holding both routes to the same standard.

CPT also plays a distinct role in the international student journey. It can provide a first opportunity to understand how a US workplace operates while a student is still enrolled and supported by their university

CPT also plays a distinct role in the international student journey. It can provide a first opportunity to understand how a US workplace operates while a student is still enrolled and supported by their university. That experience can deepen the education itself, regardless of whether the student later remains in the United States or takes what they have learned elsewhere.

Universities have a responsibility to prevent CPT from being used as a substitute work visa. That requires careful review of the academic connection and meaningful oversight. A narrow rule applied across every program, however, can exclude legitimate placements along with questionable ones. Policy should distinguish genuine academic training from employment dressed up as study.

Predictability is part of the promise

Policy changes land first on individual students. Students often accept offers and arrange their academic schedules months before a placement begins. When authorisation changes late, they can lose an opportunity that cannot simply be recreated the following term.

The uncertainty also weighs heavily on the university staff responsible for applying immigration rules to individual cases. They must use professional judgment while protecting each student’s status and their institution’s ability to enroll international students. When the consequences of getting a decision wrong are high, unclear guidance naturally leads to caution. Legitimate opportunities may be lost even where the academic purpose is strong.

Universities cannot respond instantly by rewriting degree requirements. Curriculum changes require faculty approval and advance notice, while employers plan recruitment well before students are due to start. A workable transition needs precise definitions and enough time to implement changes responsibly, informed by consultation with the institutions that administer the rules.

The wider lesson reaches beyond CPT. Relative demand for on-campus study in the US rose by 40% in the week after the midterm elections, following two years of decline. The figure tracks browsing interest rather than applications or enrollment, but it offers an early indication of how quickly perceptions can shift when policy expectations change.

Where they ultimately choose to study has consequences for universities and the wider US economy. International students are estimated to have contributed $41.77 billion to the US economy and supported almost 333,000 jobs in 2025/26. The United States should enforce its standards through a process that students and universities can understand and plan around.

Practical training is part of the value of US higher education. Protecting the integrity of that opportunity and providing predictable rules are compatible goals. If we want international students to commit their talent and resources to the United States, the commitments made to them must carry weight too.

title: Manifest Global acquires Mindler’s career guidance business
summary:
The Singapore-based group plans to extend the Indian company’s career assessment from Cialfo schools in India to users of BridgeU and FlowAI, and expand certification for counsellors in India and abroad.

The post Manifest Global acquires Mindler’s career guidance business appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
Manifest Global has acquired the career guidance business of India’s Mindler after the two companies worked together as partners over the past year.

The group announced the deal on November 19 without disclosing financial terms. Mindler founder and CEO Prateek Bhargava and his team will continue to run the business, and its school partners will retain access to the products and programs they already use.

Rohan Pasari, Manifest’s founder and CEO, told The PIE News that the partnership had allowed the group to test its view that career exploration should come before university choice.

“AI is changing what work looks like, and families increasingly want to understand where an education leads before deciding which path to take,” said Pasari.

“That view shapes everything we are building at Manifest. Our work starts long before a university application and continues through to where talent ultimately ends up working.”

Founded in 2015, Mindler uses psychometric assessments to help students explore careers based on their interests, aptitudes, personality and working style.

Pasari said its assessment was developed and validated with more than 12,000 students and matches students to more than 400 career pathways.

Mindler says it has reached more than three million students. Bhargava told The PIE that the company works directly with more than 150 schools, with a further 150-plus partners using its assessment with their own students.

Bhargava said 75,000 educators have taken part in Mindler’s training programs, which range from introductory courses to full career coach certification.

Mindler offers its International Certified Career Coach program under a credentialing arrangement with the US National Career Development Association.

Pasari said the company would initially look to expand certification through schools already using Cialfo and BridgeU in India. Beyond India, Pasari identified Southeast Asia, China, the Middle East and Western Europe as markets where Manifest plans to introduce Mindler’s products through its school and recruitment partners, with coach certification to follow.

The companies also plan to work with governments to bring career and college counselling into public schools.

AI is changing what work looks like, and families increasingly want to understand where an education leads before deciding which path to take

Rohan Pasari, Manifest Global

Manifest launched in January 2025 as the parent company of Cialfo, Explore and Kaaiser and expanded its school guidance business that April when it acquired BridgeU from Kaplan.

Its August acquisition of EduGo Abroad added an Indian consultancy with university and college partners across 18 European countries.

Bhargava said Cialfo schools in India already have access to Mindler’s assessment, while BridgeU and FlowAI users could gain access as early as the first quarter of 2027, with market-specific versions to follow.

“A career assessment is only as effective as its understanding of the student taking it, and a global assessment must understand a student in London as well as it understands one in Delhi,” Bhargava told The PIE. “That is the standard we are building towards.”

title: Record £400m Erasmus+ funding opens international opportunities for UK
summary:
More than 100,000 people across the UK are expected to benefit from international education, training and development opportunities as applications open for a record £400 million in Erasmus+ funding.

The post Record £400m Erasmus+ funding opens international opportunities for UK appeared first on The PIE News.
full_text:
More than 100,000 people across the UK are expected to benefit from international education, training and development opportunities as applications open for a record £400 million in Erasmus+ funding.

The British Council, which serves as the UK National Agency for Erasmus+, has announced that organisations can now apply for grants across six sectors: higher education, schools, vocational education and training, adult education, youth and sport.

The program supports international placements, exchanges and partnerships, helping people develop new skills, gain valuable experience and build connections across Europe and beyond.

Funding is available to a wide range of UK organisations, including universities, colleges, schools, training providers, youth groups and grassroots sports organisations.

Higher education institutions accredited under the Erasmus Charter for Higher Education (ECHE) will have access to approximately £170m, while around £100m has been allocated to vocational education and training providers.

Schools will be able to apply for a share of approximately £70m, with £30m available for youth activities and £20m for adult education.

For the first time, UK sports organisations will also be eligible for Erasmus+ funding, with approximately £2m earmarked for grassroots sport.

Grants can help cover travel, accommodation, living expenses, course fees, visas, language learning and other costs associated with international education and training activities. Initial funding for most projects is expected to be awarded in summer 2027.

Although Erasmus+ is widely associated with university students studying abroad, the program offers opportunities for people of all ages and backgrounds.

Activities can include short-term placements, job-shadowing, workshops, cultural exchanges, volunteering, remote learning and professional development.

Additional financial support is available to help people who might otherwise face barriers to participation, including those with disabilities, additional learning needs or health conditions, unpaid carers, people from disadvantaged backgrounds and those living in remote or rural communities.

Maddalaine Ansell, Erasmus+ UK National Agency director, said: “Erasmus+ represents a huge investment in education and training, youth and sport in the UK. We want to see applications for funding from every postcode and from every sector – with students in higher and further education, apprentices, trainees, adult learners, school pupils, young people and the professionals and volunteers who work with them all developing skills for work and life.”

Minister of State for Skills Jacqui Smith welcomed the opportunities the program would create for students, apprentices and teachers.

Erasmus+ will open doors for a new generation – giving students, apprentices and teachers across the country the chance to broaden their horizons and experience the wider world, while building new skills, growing in confidence and forming new relationship

Jacqui Smith, UK skills minister

“Erasmus+ will open doors for a new generation – giving students, apprentices and teachers across the country the chance to broaden their horizons and experience the wider world, while building new skills, growing in confidence and forming new relationships,” she said.

“It’s not just for those doing language degrees. From schools to colleges, and from pupils to sports coaches, I want everyone to seize this opportunity, build international partnerships and ensure these life-changing experiences reach those who stand to gain the most,” the minister continued.

Minister for European relations Hamish Falconer MP said the UK’s association with Erasmus+ would also benefit apprentices, teachers and community organisations, allowing them to develop skills overseas that could support their communities and careers back home.

title: When an Anatomy Practical Exam Becomes a Learning Event
summary:
In higher education, we often say we want students to move beyond memorization. Yet many of our exams still reward exactly that: recognize the correct answer, write it down, move to the next question.  In my own teaching, I began noticing a familiar pattern. Many students were doing well, but the lower-performing tail of the […]

The post When an Anatomy Practical Exam Becomes a Learning Event appeared first on Faculty Focus | Higher Ed Teaching & Learning.
full_text:
In higher education, we often say we want students to move beyond memorization. Yet many of our exams still reward exactly that: recognize the correct answer, write it down, move to the next question.

In my own teaching, I began noticing a familiar pattern. Many students were doing well, but the lower-performing tail of the class seemed to be getting longer. These were not students who lacked potential. Many were working hard, but they were struggling to connect isolated facts into usable understanding.

That raised a simple question for me: Was my exam only measuring the gap, or could it help reduce it?

This question led me to redesign one practical exam using a format I now think of as collaborative reasoning with individual accountability. The goal was not to make the exam easier. The goal was to make students’ thinking more visible before they had to answer on their own.

The Problem With “Just Make it a Group Exam”

I did not want to simply turn the exam into a group test. That can create legitimate concerns: uneven participation, stronger students carrying weaker students, and students receiving credit for answers they may not understand.

At the same time, I did not want to ignore the value of peer discussion. Students often learn a great deal when they hear how classmates approach a problem, especially when the task requires reasoning rather than simple recall.

So the challenge became this: How do we let students benefit from discussion without removing individual accountability?

The solution was a two-phase exam station:

Group reasoning first

Individual answers second

Students could talk through the material, but every student still had to answer independently.

How the Format Worked

At each station, students first saw a set of tagged structures. Importantly, they did not see the questions yet.

They had a short period of time to discuss everything they knew about those structures. They could talk about identification, function, relationships, applications, or anything else that might matter.

Then the timer went off. Discussion stopped. Students flipped over the question card.

At that point, each student answered the questions individually. No talking. No group answer sheet. No shared score.

The format was simple:

Students examine the material.

Students discuss as a group.

Questions are revealed.

Students answer individually.

The group phase created the learning opportunity. The individual phase preserved accountability.

What Changed

When we compared student performance on a traditional exam with performance on the collaborative format, overall performance improved. But the more meaningful result was not the class average.

The biggest improvement came from students in the lower-performing quartiles.

That mattered to me. My goal was not to inflate grades across the board. My goal was to support the students who were struggling to make connections. The discussion seemed to give those students access to how their peers were reasoning before they had to retrieve and apply the information themselves.

The strongest students did not show the same level of improvement, likely because they were already performing near the top. But the lower tail moved, and that was the point.

What Students Thought

Student feedback was generally positive, especially around learning. Many students reported that discussion helped them understand the material more clearly and supported their individual answers.

But their feedback was not universally enthusiastic, and that is important.

Some students felt the individual answer period was too short. Others raised concerns about fairness and group dynamics. Some preferred the traditional format. Some preferred the collaborative format. Some had no strong preference.

That tension is useful. It tells us that the format has promise, but the details matter.

In future versions, I would keep the core structure but refine the timing. I would also be more explicit about expectations during the discussion phase:

Every student should contribute.

The goal is to explain reasoning, not just name answers.

Discussion should focus on relationships and applications.

Once the individual phase begins, all discussion stops.

This is not a shortcut. It is a structured thinking phase.

Why This May Work in Undergraduate Courses

Although I developed this format in an anatomy practical, the idea is not limited to anatomy or professional programs. It can work in many undergraduate courses where students need to apply concepts rather than simply recall facts.

In biology, students could examine a diagram, specimen, data figure, or microscopy image together before answering individual questions.

In chemistry, students could discuss a reaction mechanism, molecular structure, or lab scenario before individually predicting products or explaining errors.

In physics, students could reason through a diagram, graph, or conceptual problem before each student solves a related question independently.

In engineering, students could discuss a design constraint, system diagram, or failure scenario before individually explaining the next step.

In mathematics or statistics, students could discuss a problem setup, dataset, or model choice before independently completing a calculation or interpretation.

In humanities and social sciences, students could discuss a short passage, case, artifact, primary source, or policy scenario before writing an individual response.

The key is the sequence: Students discuss before seeing the questions. Then they answer individually.

That sequence matters. If students see the questions first, they may simply divide the work. If they discuss the material first, they must activate what they know more broadly. They prepare each other to think, not just to copy.

Why This Matters for Undergraduate Programs

Many undergraduate programs are concerned with persistence, DFW rates, first-generation student support, and performance gaps in gateway courses. Often, the students who struggle most are not unwilling to learn; they may simply lack access to the reasoning strategies that more experienced or confident students are already using.

This format gives them a brief window into those strategies.

They hear how peers identify key features, eliminate wrong ideas, connect concepts, and decide what matters. Then they must answer on their own.

That is the balance I find valuable: support without removing responsibility.

Practical Tips for Trying This Yourself

Faculty do not need to redesign an entire course to try this approach. Start small.

Use it for one quiz, one exam section, one lab practical, or a few problem-solving stations.

I would recommend:

Keep groups small: three to five students.

Hide the questions during the discussion phase.

Use a visible timer.

Keep individual answers short.

Use mostly foundational questions with a few deeper application questions.

Avoid group scores.

Collect feedback immediately afterward.

Tell students why you are using the format.

The last point matters. Students may assume group work means the exam will be easier. I tell them directly: this is not designed to make the exam easier. It is designed to make the thinking more visible.

Final Thought

Assessment does not have to be separate from learning. With careful design, it can become part of the learning process itself.

The lesson for me was not that every exam should become collaborative. They should not. The lesson was more practical: when students are allowed to reason together before answering individually, struggling students may get the support they need without removing accountability.

That is the kind of assessment worth building.

Dr. Pradeep Malreddy is a Clinical Associate Professor at Kansas State University, specializing in Anatomy and Histology. Holding a DVM from India and an MS from Kansas State, he brings a blend of clinical and academic expertise. He has additional certifications in Medical Education Research and Online Teaching from AAMC and Harvard. Dr. Malreddy has developed a One-Year Master’s Program at K-State and teaches courses in anatomy, histology, and physiology. His research focuses on anatomy education, eye-tracking technology, and active learning. An active member of professional organizations like the American Association of Veterinary Anatomists, he has received accolades for teaching excellence and diversity initiatives. He was recently honored with Fellowship in the United Kingdom’s prestigious Academy of Medical Educators.

title: Kurz eingeordnet: Das neue Education and Skills Package der EU
summary:
Die EU-Kommission hat das neue Education and Skills Package vorgestellt. Welche Schwerpunkte setzt das Maßnahmenpaket bei KI, digitaler Souveränität und der Zukunft der Bildung – und was bedeutet das für Hochschulen?

The post Kurz eingeordnet: Das neue Education and Skills Package der EU appeared first on Hochschulforum Digitalisierung.
full_text:
Mit dem neuen Education and Skills Package hat die Europäische Kommission Anfang November 2026 ein umfangreiches Maßnahmenpaket für Bildung und Kompetenzen vorgestellt. Der Anlass dafür sind unter anderem die jüngsten PISA-Ergebnisse, die teils auf einen Rückgang grundlegender Kompetenzen in der EU hinweisen, aber auch die weiterhin zunehmende Bedeutung von KI, der digitalen Transformation und der Fachkräftesicherung.

Da sich viele Maßnahmen ausdrücklich an Schulen, Lehrkräfte und die berufliche Aus- und Weiterbildung richten, scheint die Relevanz für Hochschulen auf den ersten Blick überschaubar. Geplant sind unter anderem neue European School Alliances, eine EU Teachers Agenda, Teacher Academies 2.0 sowie ein europäischer Rahmen für AI Literacy im Schulbereich.

Doch es lohnt sich ein genauerer Blick. Denn das Paket zeigt nicht nur, welche Herausforderungen die Europäische Kommission aktuell im Bildungsbereich sieht. Es macht auch sichtbar, welche Leitideen die europäische Bildungspolitik künftig stärker prägen könnten. Einige davon gehen deutlich über schulische und berufliche Bildung hinaus.

Wichtig ist dabei zu betonen, dass Bildung eine Zuständigkeit der Mitgliedstaaten bleibt und die im Paket enthaltenen Empfehlungen nicht verbindlich sind. Die Europäische Kommission setzt hier lediglich Impulse für Zusammenarbeit und gemeinsame Entwicklung auf europäischer Ebene.

Das Muster ist bekannt: Einzelne Maßnahmen sind oft stark auf bestimmte Bildungsbereiche zugeschnitten. Gleichzeitig lassen sich daraus breitere Entwicklungen auch für andere Bereiche herauslesen.

Beim Education and Skills Package fällt auf, dass mehrere seiner Dokumente um ähnliche Fragen kreisen. Wie können Lernende Kompetenzen erwerben, die sie in einer zunehmend von KI geprägten Gesellschaft benötigen? Welche Rolle spielen dabei Lehrkräfte und Bildungsinstitutionen? Wie können digitale Technologien sinnvoll genutzt werden, ohne pädagogische Ziele aus dem Blick zu verlieren? Und welche digitalen Infrastrukturen braucht Europa dafür?

Das Paket verdeutlicht zudem den Trend, dass die Europäische Kommission digitale Bildung weniger als Frage technischer Ausstattung behandelt, sondern zunehmend Kompetenzen, pädagogische Unterstützung, institutionelle Rahmenbedingungen und digitale Souveränität in den Mittelpunkt rückt.

Besonders sichtbar wird diese Entwicklung beim Thema AI Literacy. Im Paket wird angekündigt, dass auf Grundlage des bereits veröffentlichten EU-OECD AI Literacy Frameworks Referenz-Lernergebnisse und Orientierung für die Leistungsbewertung entwickelt werden. Zudem soll ab dem Schuljahr 2027/28 ein europäisches AI Literacy Certificate pilotiert werden.

Bemerkenswert ist dabei weniger die Einführung des Zertifikats selbst, sondern die zugrundeliegende Perspektive. KI-Kompetenz wird im Package nicht als Spezialwissen verstanden. Stattdessen stehen Fragen des Verständnisses, der kritischen Einordnung und der verantwortungsvollen Nutzung von KI im Vordergrund und das für alle Schülerinnen und Schüler.

Diese Entwicklung lässt sich auch außerhalb des Schulbereichs beobachten. Die Diskussion hat sich in den letzten Jahren verschoben. Nachdem zunächst vor allem neue Tools und ihre Möglichkeiten im Mittelpunkt standen, rücken inzwischen Fragen nach Kompetenzen, Verantwortung und institutionellen Rahmenbedingungen stärker in den Vordergrund.

Für Hochschulen ist das keine neue Debatte. Dennoch zeigt das Paket, dass AI Literacy auf europäischer Ebene zunehmend als grundlegende Bildungsaufgabe verstanden wird und nicht als Nischenthema.

Ein weiterer interessanter Aspekt findet sich im European Digital Infrastrucure Consortium on Education (EDU-EDIC). Dieses soll Mitgliedstaaten dabei unterstützen, gemeinsame digitale Infrastrukturen für Bildung aufzubauen. Genannt werden unter anderem vertrauenswürdige KI-Dienste, gemeinsame Datenschutzstandards, Interoperabilität und die Unterstützung europäischer EdTech-Anbieter.

Auch diese Initiative richtet sich vor allem an den Schulbereich. Gleichzeitig wird hier eine Entwicklung sichtbar, die in den vergangenen Jahren immer wichtiger geworden ist: Digitale Bildung wird zunehmend auch als Infrastrukturfrage verstanden. Es geht nicht mehr nur darum, welche Anwendungen genutzt werden. Ebenso relevant werden Fragen nach Datenhoheit, technischer Abhängigkeit, gemeinsamen Standards und der Fähigkeit Europas, eigene digitale Lösungen zu entwickeln und zu betreiben.

Gerade im Zusammenhang mit generativer KI gewinnt diese Perspektive an Bedeutung. Das Education and Skills Package verknüpft technologische Innovation und digitale Souveränität noch stärker als frühere Initiativen.

Ein wiederkehrendes Thema im Package ist die Rolle von Lehrkräften. Mit der vorgeschlagenen EU Teachers Agenda und den geplanten Teacher Academies 2.0 reagiert die Europäische Kommission auf Lehrkräftemangel, steigende Anforderungen und die fortschreitende Digitalisierung. Dabei geht es nicht nur um Arbeitsbedingungen und Nachwuchsgewinnung, sondern auch um professionelle Entwicklung, digitale Kompetenzen und den Umgang mit KI.

Das Paket verbindet technologische Fragen konsequent mit der Professionalisierung von Lehrenden. Das verdeutlicht, dass die Kommission die digitale Transformation nicht als Technologievorhaben versteht, sondern als Bildungsaufgabe, die ohne entsprechend qualifiziertes Personal nicht gelingen kann.

Dies ist auch im Hochschulkontext bekannt. Die Einführung neuer Technologien verändert Lehr- und Lernprozesse nicht automatisch. Entscheidend bleibt, dass die Lehrenden sie einsetzen, reflektieren und in ihre Lehre einbetten.

Das neue Education and Skills Package ist vor allem ein Paket für Schulen, Lehrkräfte und berufliche Bildungseinrichtungen.
